title: The log in the fire (Dark Night 2.10)
hookLine: wet wood hisses and blackens before it becomes flame

cards: Put a damp log on a campfire and wait for a big, cheerful flame. Instead you get hissing. Popping.
Water bubbling out of the ends of the log. Gray smoke in your eyes. The bark goes black and ugly.
It smells bad. It looks like the fire is ruining the wood, and you start to wonder if it'll ever catch. Then, slowly, it does.
John of the Cross uses exactly that kind of fire.

teach.b: First, the stages. In the Dark Night, book two, chapter ten, John walks through it. When fire first touches a log, it doesn't set it ablaze.
It dries it, driving out the dampness, so the wood seems to weep. Then it blackens it, makes it dark and ugly, even gives off a bad smell. Only as it dries does the fire give it heat and light.
At the end, the wood becomes fire itself, as bright and hot as the flame.
Second, the log is the soul.

teach.h: THE FIRE DRAWS OUT WHAT WAS THERE.
teach.b: The fire is God's love. When that love first gets close, John says, the soul doesn't feel lit up. It feels worse.
It suddenly sees its own damp and dark places, faults it didn't know it had. Third, the surprise. Here's John's key point.
The fire isn't making the wood ugly. The ugliness was already in the wood. The fire is drawing it out, so it can be burned away.
So when someone who's trying to love God suddenly feels more aware of their failings, John says, that's often not a sign of getting worse.
It's the smoke. The fire is working. Fourth, the flame.
The same fire that hurt at first becomes the one that delights. The log doesn't stay a log with a fire next to it. It becomes flame.
John wrote a whole other poem about that end, the Living Flame of Love. For John, the smoke is part of the burning.

how: Catholic spiritual directors use John's image of the log in the fire to reassure people who feel more aware of their faults as they grow in prayer, and his Living Flame of Love is read as the fulfillment of that image.

o: the soul fully alight, once God's love has burned through it
the candle lit at Easter to stand for the risen Christ
a Carmelite rule for keeping silence at night

games.q: what's inside the fire — tap the pairs.
p: faults drawn out to be burned

s: John says the fire makes the wood ugly
the ugliness was already there. the fire draws it out so it can burn away.
noticing more faults can be a sign the fire is working
John says it's often the smoke, not a sign of getting worse.
John wrote a separate poem about the flame at the end

games.q: you've been praying seriously for a year, and suddenly you notice your faults more than ever. what does John say?
o: it may be the smoke: the fire drawing out what was there.
games.why: John says the fire first dries and blackens the wood before it becomes flame. the smoke means the fire is working.

practice: Think of one fault you've been noticing in yourself lately, maybe more than before: impatience, envy, a sharp tongue. Instead of beating yourself up, picture it as smoke rising off a log, damp coming out so it can burn clean.
If you pray, let God's love keep working on it; if you don't, be gentle with yourself, the way you'd wait out a smoky fire.

wordCard.voice: Living Flame. What the log becomes once God's love has dried and blackened it: the title of John's other poem, naming the soul fully alight. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish: oh living flame of love. the first line of John's poem about the fire's end, when the wood becomes flame.

carryVoice: Your line: first smoke, then flame. The ugliness was already there; the fire just brings it out. Until tomorrow.
